1. A cart X of mass 3.0 kg moving at $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides with a stationary cart Y of mass 6.0 kg. A spring is attached to X as shown.
[Diagram: cart X with a spring on its front moving at $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards stationary cart Y on a horizontal track]
The graph shows the velocities of X and Y before, during and after the collision.
[Graph: $v$ / m s$^{-1}$ (−2 to 6) against $t$ / ms (0 to 60). X: constant 6 until 10 ms, falls through 2 at 30 ms to −2 by 50 ms. Y: 0 until 10 ms, rises through 2 at 30 ms to 4 by 50 ms. Arrow marks duration of collision from 10 ms to 50 ms]
The collision lasted for 40 ms.
(a) Show that the collision is elastic. [2]
(b) Determine
(i) the magnitude of the average force exerted on Y, [2]
(ii) the average power delivered to Y, [2]
(iii) the elastic energy stored in the spring at $t = 30$ ms. [2]

2.text_clean:
2. (a) Describe the mechanism of heat transfer by conduction. [2]
The diagram shows a wall separating the inside of a room from the outside. The temperature of the room is kept constant by a heater.
[Diagram: wall of area 18 m$^2$ and thickness 0.25 m; inside 22 °C, outside 13 °C]
The following data are available:
Thickness of wall = 0.25 m
Area of wall = 18 m$^2$
Thermal conductivity of wall = $1.3\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$
Constant room temperature = 22 °C
Constant outside temperature = 13 °C
(b) Estimate the rate at which thermal energy leaves the room through the wall giving the answer with an appropriate unit. [2]
(c) At night the outside temperature falls below 13 °C. The heater is turned off at time $t = 0$. The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the temperature $T$ of the room.
[Graph: $T$ / °C (0 to 25) against $t$ / min (0 to 120); curve decays from 22 °C at $t=0$ to about 10 °C at 20 min, levelling off at about 6 °C from 60 min to 120 min]
(i) Outline why the magnitude of the gradient of the graph decreases. [1]
(ii) The pressure and volume of the air in the room remain constant but the number of molecules has increased. Determine the percentage increase in the number of molecules of air in the room between $t = 0$ and $t = 120$ min. [3]
(d) Discuss how the second law of thermodynamics applies to the situation of the room cooling down. [2]

3.text_clean:
3. Two oppositely charged parallel plates are a distance 8.0 cm apart. The potential difference between the plates is 120 V. An alpha particle is placed on the positively charged plate and released from rest. Gravity is ignored.
[Diagram: horizontal parallel plates, positive on top, negative below, 8.0 cm apart, p.d. 120 V; alpha particle on the positive plate]
(a) Calculate the electric field between the plates. [1]
(b) (i) Show that the acceleration of the alpha particle is about $7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. [2]
(ii) Calculate the time taken for the alpha particle to reach the negative plate. [2]
(iii) State, in eV, the kinetic energy of the alpha particle when it arrives at the negative plate. [1]
(c) A magnetic field directed into the plane of the page is now established between the plates. An alpha particle enters the region between the plates with a horizontal speed of $5.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The particle is not deflected.
[Diagram: plates (+ top, − bottom) with magnetic field into page (crosses); alpha particle entering horizontally from the left]
Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field. [2]
(d) The alpha particle in (c) is replaced by an electron. The electron enters the region between the plates with the same velocity as the alpha particle.
Draw, on the diagram, the path of the electron. [1]
[Diagram: same plates and field, electron entering horizontally from the left]

4.text_clean:
4. Two sources of light produce an interference pattern on a screen.
(a) Explain why the two sources need to be coherent for the interference pattern to be observed. [2]
(b) Light of wavelength 720 nm is incident on two narrow slits that are separated by 0.12 mm. An interference pattern is observed on a screen. P$_1$ and P$_2$ are the points of destructive interference closest to the central maximum M.
[Diagram: light incident on double slit; lines from slits to P$_1$ and P$_2$ on screen either side of M, subtending angle $\varphi$]
(i) Calculate, in radians, the angular separation $\varphi$ of P$_1$ and P$_2$. [2]
(ii) Suggest how energy conservation is consistent with the fact that the energy at P$_1$ and P$_2$ is zero. [1]
A beam of light containing all wavelengths in the range [550 nm, 650 nm] is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The grating has 580 lines per mm. A diffraction pattern is observed on a screen as shown.
[Diagram: light incident on diffraction grating; central point M on screen]
(c) Outline why the interference at M is constructive. [1]
(d) Determine the largest order of the diffraction pattern in which all the wavelengths in the incident beam are present. [3]

5.text_clean:
5. (a) Outline why Compton scattering offers better evidence for the particle nature of light than the photoelectric effect. [2]
A photon of wavelength $6.40 \times 10^{-12}$ m and energy 0.194 MeV is incident on an electron at rest. The photon scatters at an angle $\theta$ with wavelength $7.47 \times 10^{-12}$ m. The electron recoils.
[Diagram: incident photon moving towards electron at rest; after collision, scattered photon at angle $\theta$ above the original direction and recoiling electron moving below it]
(b) Outline why the wavelength of the scattered photon is longer than that of the incident photon. [2]
(c) (i) Show that the energy of the scattered photon is about 0.17 MeV. [1]
(ii) Calculate the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron. [1]
(iii) For an electron, $\frac{h}{m_e c} = 2.43 \times 10^{-12}$ m. Determine $\theta$. [2]

6.text_clean:
6. Spacecraft S leaves Earth with speed 0.60c on the way to a planet P. As measured by Earth, P is at a distance of 30 ly from Earth. The diagram shows the spacetime axes of Earth ($x$, $ct$) and of S ($x'$, $ct'$).
[Spacetime diagram: $ct$ / ly (0 to 140) against $x$ / ly (0 to 140); $ct'$ axis through origin with slope 1/0.60, $x'$ axis through origin with slope 0.60]
(a) S arrives at P after 50 years according to Earth. Calculate the time at which S arrives at P according to S clocks. [2]
(b) When S arrives at P, S sends a radio signal back to Earth.
(i) Draw, on the spacetime diagram, the world line of the signal from when it is emitted until it is received on Earth. [1]
(ii) Determine, using the spacetime diagram or otherwise, the time of travel of the signal according to S. [3]

7.text_clean:
7. The following data are available for the Sun when it entered the main sequence.
Mass = $2.0 \times 10^{30}$ kg
Radius = $7.0 \times 10^{8}$ m
Surface temperature = 5800 K
Core temperature = $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ K
Core density = $1.6 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
(a) (i) State and explain which of the above features make nuclear fusion in the Sun possible. [3]
(ii) Outline how the Sun maintains its equilibrium state. [2]
(b) The following sequence of nuclear fusion reactions takes place in the Sun.
Stage 1: ${}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{0}_{1}\bar{e}^{+} + {}^{0}_{0}\nu$
Stage 2: ${}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{0}_{0}\gamma$
Stage 3: ${}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + 2 \times {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}$
The nuclear mass of ${}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}$ is 1.007276 u and that of ${}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}$ is 2.013550 u. Estimate the energy released in stage 1 of these reactions. [2]
(c) The Sun will leave the main sequence when it has converted 10 % of its hydrogen mass into helium. The total energy released in the reactions in (b) is $4.3 \times 10^{-12}$ J. The current luminosity of the Sun is $3.8 \times 10^{26}$ W. When the Sun entered the main sequence its hydrogen mass was $1.5 \times 10^{30}$ kg.
(i) Show that the Sun will stay on the main sequence for about $8 \times 10^{9}$ years. [3]
(ii) State one assumption that was made in getting the answer to (c)(i). [1]
(iii) Estimate the total mass lost by the Sun in this time. [2]
(d) The surface temperature of the Sun is 5800 K. Determine the peak wavelength in the Sun's spectrum. [2]
(e) The Sun rotates about its axis. P is a point on the Sun's equator.
[Diagram: Sun of radius R rotating; point P on the equator at the top, moving towards Earth, which is to the right]
A particular spectral line of hydrogen from a laboratory source has wavelength 656.2797 nm. The same spectral line emitted from P has wavelength 656.2753 nm when measured on Earth.
(i) Explain this observation. [2]
(ii) Calculate the period of revolution of the Sun. [3]

8.text_clean:
8. (a) A cylindrical spacecraft of cross-sectional area $S$ moves with velocity $v$. The spacecraft enters a region of dust of density $\rho$. All the dust that comes into contact with the forward cross-sectional area of the spacecraft sticks to the spacecraft increasing its mass.
[Diagram: cylindrical spacecraft with front face area S moving with velocity v into a block-shaped region of dust]
(i) Show that in time $\Delta t$ the mass of the spacecraft will increase by an amount $\rho S v \Delta t$. [1]
(ii) Deduce that the spacecraft will experience a drag force $\rho S v^2$ opposite to its velocity. [2]
(b) A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around Earth. Earth has mass $M$.
(i) Show that the total energy of the satellite is given by $E_T = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$. [2]
(ii) The satellite experiences a drag force due to the atmosphere of Earth. With reference to the results in (a) and (b)(i), state and explain the likely fate of this satellite. [4]
(c) The graph shows the variation with time of the height of the International Space Station (ISS) during a 30-day period.
[Graph: height / km (416.0 to 419.0) against time / days (0 to 30); straight line falling from about 418.7 km at day 0 to about 416.2 km at day 30]
The following data are available:
Mass of Earth = $5.98 \times 10^{24}$ kg
Mass of the ISS = $4.20 \times 10^{5}$ kg
Radius of the Earth = $6.38 \times 10^{6}$ m
For the 30-day period indicated in the graph the loss of total energy of the ISS is $4.5 \times 10^{9}$ J.
(i) Calculate the average rate at which the energy of the ISS is being dissipated. [2]
(ii) Show, using the average height during the 30-day period, that the speed of the ISS is about $8 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. [2]
(iii) Estimate the increase in the temperature of the ISS assuming all the lost energy went into thermal energy of the ISS. Take the specific heat capacity of the ISS to be $500\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. [2]
(iv) Estimate, using the answers to (c)(i) and (c)(ii), the average drag force that acted on the ISS. [3]
(d) At the end of the 30-day period, rockets are fired to bring the ISS back to its initial height. The energy density of liquid hydrogen rocket fuel is $8.5 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{MJ\,m^{-3}}$.
Estimate the volume of fuel needed. [2]
